theme: Data-hosting mirrors pointed at from GitHub: Zenodo, Figshare, Harvard Dataverse, HuggingFace, Kaggle, Mendeley Data collections on Airbnb, STR, hotels, tourism

candidates.name: alujjdnd/Airbnb-Mar-2022-2023
candidates.what_it_holds: 16,548,869 rows of Airbnb reviews (listing_id, id, date, reviewer_id, reviewer_name, comments) for Buenos Aires, Argentina, spanning 2011 through early 2023, 9.48GB, CSV + auto-converted Parquet, MIT licence. Despite the repo name (Mar 2022-2023) the review dates go back to 2011.
candidates.why_useful: Buenos Aires is a LatAm market not in our 13-city Inside Airbnb panel, and the review history predates our earliest Inside Airbnb dumps (Dec 2022). Reviews-based volume proxies (our 123-market stays index approach) could be extended to this market/period, and it is a genuine multi-year historical review archive of the kind gap #1 asks for (older-than-2023 data), just for a market we don't currently cover.

candidates.name: kraina/airbnb
candidates.what_it_holds: 51,700 Airbnb listing rows across 10 European cities (Amsterdam etc.), split into weekday/weekend snapshots, with realSum (price), room type, capacity, host status, cleanliness/satisfaction scores, distance to metro/attractions, amenity indices, lat/long. CC-BY-4.0. This is the well-known 'Airbnb Prices in European Cities' dataset re-hosted with Croissant/SQL support.
candidates.why_useful: A static but clean 10-city European cross-section (price vs. distance/amenity structure) that is not in our current 13-city Inside Airbnb panel composition; useful as an ADR-structure cross-check for EMEA pricing work, though it is a single-period snapshot, not a time series.
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: overlaps cities already in our 13-city Inside Airbnb panel (Paris, London, Barcelona, Rome) but different vintage/fields

candidates.name: michaelmallari/airbnb-* (US/Canada city series)
candidates.what_it_holds: A family of per-city Airbnb listing datasets (Denver, Asheville, Austin, Bozeman, Nashville, New York, Portland, San Diego, Twin Cities, Washington DC, Toronto, Vancouver, and more), updated January 2024, mirroring Inside Airbnb-style listing exports per market.
candidates.why_useful: Adds cities outside our 13-city panel (Denver, Asheville, Bozeman, Twin Cities, DC, Toronto, Vancouver) at a Jan 2024 vintage; could extend the US/Canada cross-section, though vintage overlaps what Inside Airbnb itself would have had at that date (not older/rarer).
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: likely re-hosts Inside Airbnb source data we can already pull directly for cities we care about; only the extra cities (Denver, Asheville, Bozeman, Twin Cities, DC, Toronto, Vancouver) are new

candidates.name: tomslee/airbnb-data-collection
candidates.what_it_holds: A pre-Inside-Airbnb (2015-2019) Python/PostgreSQL+PostGIS scraper that queried airbnb.com by neighborhood/zipcode/bounding-box search and stored results in a `room`/`survey` schema. Author states it is 'no longer maintained' (site changes broke it around v3.6, last activity ~July 2019, 250 commits). MIT licence. No committed CSV data in the repo itself, but this was the tool behind Tom Slee's own historical Airbnb scrape archives (2015-2017) that predate Inside Airbnb's own launch.
candidates.why_useful: Documents the method/schema used for the earliest known independent Airbnb listing archives (2015-2017), which is the vintage gap #1 explicitly wants filled; useful as a pointer to go find Slee's actual historical CSV dumps (hosted on his now-defunct site / mirrors) rather than as a runnable scraper today, and per repo rules any live scrape of airbnb.com is a ToS call for a human anyway.
candidates.time_coverage: tool active 2015-2019; no data files committed in this repo

candidates.name: rsanjabi/short-term-rentals-warehouse
candidates.what_it_holds: A data-engineering portfolio project: Python extract/load scripts pulling Inside Airbnb listings plus Kaggle 'World Cities Population and Location' and Kaggle 'Cost of Living Indices' (Numbeo) into a Snowflake warehouse with DBT transforms and Metabase dashboards. README claims 'over 35 million records from 2015-2020' across the three sources, global city coverage. No raw data files committed to the repo itself (external Snowflake/Kaggle sources).
candidates.why_useful: A reusable pipeline pattern for joining Inside Airbnb supply data with city-level cost-of-living/population context globally; the 2015-2020 claim suggests it may reach further back than our current dump coverage, worth checking its actual Inside Airbnb pull dates if pursued.
candidates.duplicate_of_holding: built entirely on Inside Airbnb, which we already hold; incremental value is only in the join methodology

candidates.name: kraina-ai/QuackOSM
candidates.what_it_holds: Open-source Python/CLI tool (375 stars, Apache-2.0) for reading OpenStreetMap PBF extracts directly via DuckDB, producing tabular/geoparquet output of OSM features (including tourism/accommodation/POI tags) for any region.
candidates.why_useful: A one-command way to pull OSM points of interest (hotels, short-term-rental-tagged buildings, restaurants/attractions used as tourism-density proxies) for any city/country as a free, always-current geospatial layer feeding gap #20 (geospatial POI / party-size proxies) and cross-checking Inside Airbnb listing density against broader tourism infrastructure.
candidates.time_coverage: current OSM snapshot, any historical PBF extract if available
candidates.last_activity: active (390+375 stars across kraina-ai repos, actively maintained per repo listing)

candidates.name: kraina-ai/OvertureMaestro
candidates.what_it_holds: Open-source tool (36 stars, Apache-2.0) for reading Overture Maps Foundation data (places/POI, buildings, transportation themes) with multiprocessing support.
candidates.why_useful: Overture Maps' 'places' theme includes categorized business POIs (lodging, hotels, short-term rental agencies) globally and is updated monthly/quarterly by a Linux Foundation consortium (Meta, Microsoft, Amazon, TomTom) — a free alternative/complement to commercial POI data for building geospatial tourism-density or party-size proxies (gap #20).

candidates.name: gstinoco/CITC-airbnb
candidates.what_it_holds: MIT-licensed Python pipeline (`Correlations.py`) computing Haversine distances and correlation matrices between Airbnb host/listing locations and cultural points of interest, with example host and cultural-place data bundled as tar.gz files in `Information/`. Also archived on Zenodo (10.5281 DOI family) by Gerardo Tinoco-Guerrero.
candidates.why_useful: A ready-made method for host-to-attraction proximity correlation analysis, potentially reusable for professional-host / tourism-density work, but the bundled data is example-only (city/time range not documented) so it is a method, not a new dataset.

candidates.name: everythingscraper/airbnb-scraper
candidates.what_it_holds: Python client wrapping an Apify Actor that scrapes airbnb.com to produce occupancy, ADR, and RevPAR analytics per listing/market.
candidates.why_useful: If it worked, this is exactly the realised-ADR/occupancy-for-STRs gap (#2), but it scrapes airbnb.com directly, which our rules flag as a terms-of-service decision for a human, not something to run. Catalogued as a method only, left un-run.
candidates.time_coverage: current (live scrape only, no historical data)

candidates.name: Gyódi (2021) "Airbnb and hotels during COVID-19" + "Spatial Patterns of Airbnb Offers, Hotels and Attractions" (Zenodo supplementary materials)
candidates.what_it_holds: Zenodo-hosted supplementary materials for two Kristóf Gyódi papers: one comparing Airbnb vs hotel pricing/supply flexibility across nine European cities Jan 2018-Sep 2020 (COVID shock), the other on spatial clustering of Airbnb offers vs hotels/attractions across multiple cities. The COVID record itself only has a PDF attached (no raw CSV); the spatial-patterns record is titled '...Supplementary Materials' and may carry data files not confirmed here.
candidates.why_useful: The COVID paper's 2018-2020 European city-level Airbnb/hotel supply-and-price series would predate and extend our current European coverage if the underlying data (not just the PDF) can be tracked down from the author; flagged for a human to check the actual Zenodo file list before relying on it.
candidates.size_hint: PDF only confirmed (1.2MB); data files unconfirmed

queries_run: site:github.com zenodo airbnb dataset (blocked, WebSearch budget exhausted)
dataverse harvard short-term rental dataset github (blocked, WebSearch budget exhausted)
kaggle airbnb dataset github repository review (blocked, WebSearch budget exhausted)
notes: Hit a hard wall early: this session's WebSearch tool budget was already exhausted (200/200) before any query in this run could execute, so the assigned WebSearch modality was not actually usable — every 'search' had to be done via WebFetch against static/JSON endpoints instead (GitHub topics pages, Zenodo's /api/records JSON search, Figshare's API, HuggingFace dataset-search pages). Bing and DuckDuckGo HTML fronts were fetched as a fallback but returned no usable organic results (Bing gave generic/irrelevant snippets, DuckDuckGo HTML served a bot CAPTCHA both times) and GitHub's own /search endpoint 429'd (rate-limited, likely shared across concurrent scout agents). Figshare's search API also silently ignored the search_for parameter and returned an unrelated default feed both times I tried it (climate/health articles), so Figshare is effectively uncovered by this scout - worth a retry by a scout with a working WebSearch budget or direct figshare.com browsing. Harvard Dataverse's site is JS-rendered and returned empty via WebFetch; also uncovered. Kaggle's search UI is JS-rendered and returned nothing via WebFetch; a scout with `gh`/browser access or an intact WebSearch budget should retry 'kaggle.com airbnb' and 'kaggle.com STR occupancy' directly. Given these constraints, coverage here leans on HuggingFace (which has server-rendered enough content to extract via WebFetch) and Zenodo's JSON API, both of which worked reasonably well and surfaced the Buenos Aires review archive (16.5M rows, 2011-2023) as the single most interesting find - it is outside our city panel, has a genuinely long pre-2023 history, and is a real committed dataset rather than a pointer-only paper. Recommend a follow-up scout specifically re-run this theme once the WebSearch budget resets, prioritizing Kaggle (never actually queried) and Harvard Dataverse (never actually queried) which this run could not reach at all.
